_readme: The Reading Room shelf: public-domain editions the club hosts and serves in the browser. Nothing in copyright belongs here — an un-DRM'd EPUB is downloadable by anyone who opens the reader. source_url and epub_url are deliberately null until a human has fetched the edition and confirmed the link resolves; scripts/check_library.py verifies them. Never paste a permalink you have not opened.

standard-ebooks.name: Standard Ebooks
standard-ebooks.note: Carefully typeset EPUB 3, modern markup, proper semantics — the best free editions there are. Standard Ebooks dedicates its own editorial work to the public domain (CC0), so its files can be rehosted. The download page offers a 'compatible epub' as well as the standard one; take the standard EPUB 3, which foliate-js renders best.

gutenberg.name: Project Gutenberg
gutenberg.note: Far wider catalogue, much rougher files. The texts are public domain, but the Project Gutenberg trademark licence is attached to the header they ship; use the 'no header' EPUB where offered, or strip the header before rehosting, and don't use the PG name or logo on the page.

rules: Published before 1931 clears US copyright, which is the test that matters for a US-hosted site. Say so in the rights field rather than implying worldwide public domain.

A translation carries its own copyright. Dostoevsky is public domain; a 1990s translation of him is not. Only host translations old enough to have expired — Constance Garnett, Isabel Hapgood, Samuel Butler — and name the translator on the page.
The fan page and the library book share a slug. That is what makes the 'Read it free' button appear on the fan page without anyone wiring it up by hand.
Fill source_url and epub_url only after opening them, then run scripts/check_library.py.

books.title: Frankenstein
books.author: Mary Shelley
books.note: The 1818 text and the 1831 revision are different books; say which one the edition is.

books.title: Moby-Dick
books.author: Herman Melville
books.note: Long. Worth checking how the reader handles it on a phone before publishing — it is the stress test of the shelf.

books.title: The Picture of Dorian Gray
books.author: Oscar Wilde
books.rights_basis: First published 1890; the author died in 1900.
books.note: The 1890 magazine version and the 1891 book differ by six chapters. Name the one you host.

books.title: The Great Gatsby
books.author: F. Scott Fitzgerald
books.rights: Public domain in the United States.
books.rights_basis: Published 1925; entered the US public domain on 1 January 2021. Still in copyright in some other countries — this is a US-hosted shelf.
books.note: The first of the shelf's US-only entries. The rights line on the page should say 'in the United States', not 'public domain'.

books.title: Crime and Punishment
books.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
books.rights: Public domain in the United States — original and translation both.
books.rights_basis: Original published 1866. Garnett's translation was published in 1914 and is out of US copyright; the Pevear and Volokhonsky translation most readers know is not.
books.note: Name the translator on the page. Readers who know the book will want to know which one they are getting, and the fan page's reader voices are mostly quoting a different translation.

books.title: The Brothers Karamazov
books.author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
books.rights: Public domain in the United States — original and translation both.

books.title: The Count of Monte Cristo
books.author: Alexandre Dumas
books.rights_basis: Serialised 1844–46; the standard English translation dates from 1846.
books.note: Some free editions are abridged. Check the chapter count before publishing — an abridgement passed off as the novel is worse than no edition.

books.title: Les Misérables
books.author: Victor Hugo
books.note: The largest file on the shelf. Worth watching the load time on a phone.

books.title: Dracula
books.author: Bram Stoker
books.note: No fan page yet. Epistolary structure makes it a good club read and a good test of a table of contents with many short sections.

books.title: The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes
books.author: Arthur Conan Doyle
books.note: Twelve stories, so a natural one to read a chapter at a time — the reader remembers where the club got to.

books.title: The Time Machine
books.author: H. G. Wells
books.rights: Public domain in the United States.
books.rights_basis: Published 1895. Wells died in 1946, so some countries' life-plus-70 terms ran to 2016; it is clear everywhere now, but the US date is the one this shelf relies on.
books.note: Short — a good first book for the shelf, and a good one to test on a phone in a single sitting.

books.title: Anna Karenina
books.author: Leo Tolstoy
books.rights: Public domain in the United States — original and translation both.

books.title: The Odyssey
books.author: Homer
books.rights_basis: Butler's prose translation was published in 1900. Emily Wilson's is the translation people are discussing now, and it is very much in copyright.
books.note: Name the translator prominently. A reader arriving from a conversation about the Wilson translation will otherwise think they are getting it.
